introduction: Most of these readings are words of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá spoken or written between the Russo-Japanese war and the years after the Great War. They describe war as the ruin of what parents and nations build, trace it to imaginary lines and to prejudice, hold that God does not want it, and set out a remedy: a binding pact among governments, arbitration, reduced arms, education and the equal voice of women. The quotations beside them come from the prophets and psalms, the Gospels and the Qur’an, from poets of the trenches and from statesmen. Others speak for the long tradition that has thought war sometimes necessary or even ennobling, from Heraclitus and Augustine to Clausewitz and William James, because the guide's hardest sayings deserve their strongest answers.
questions: One reading says that in war both parties are wrong and war is never necessary; another asks all governments to rise against one that breaks the pact. How do you read the two together, with Augustine and the Qur’an beside them?
What causes of war do the readings name, and which would James or Thucydides say they leave out?
What is owed to those who fought and died, in wars the readings call fruitless?
Which parts of the remedy described here have been tried since, and what has been learned?
What can one person or one community do for peace, on the showing of the last readings?

outside.why: Abner calls across the field to Joab the question the reading asks of history: shall the sword devour for ever?
Heraclitus calls war the father of all and the king of all. Is the long record of contention a sickness, or the way things have always come to be?
Julia Ward Howe spoke for mothers: our sons shall not be taken from us to unlearn the charity, mercy and patience we taught them.
Hector prays over his infant son that men may one day say of him, as he comes from battle, that he is better than his father. Why have parents wished this for the children they raised?
The Dhammapada says that victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy.
Eisenhower reckoned the cost of constant preparation: every gun made and warship launched is a theft from those who hunger.
Hardy has the dead hear that the world is as it used to be, all nations striving to make red war yet redder.
Owen asks what passing-bells there are for those who die as cattle, and answers with the guns.
Tennyson looked into the wonder of the age to come and saw the heavens fill with commerce, and with navies.
Shelley's traveller reads a conqueror's boast on a pedestal in the desert, with nothing beside it remaining.
Jesus tells his disciples they shall hear of wars and rumours of wars, nation rising against nation.
The Dhammapada holds the one who conquers himself a greater conqueror than he who defeats a thousand thousand men in battle.
Jeremiah wishes his eyes a fountain of tears, to weep day and night for the slain of his people.
Hardy's soldier finds war quaint and curious: you shoot a fellow down whom you would treat in any bar.
Whitman finds it beautiful that war and all its deeds of carnage must in time be utterly lost.
Lao Tzu calls arms, however beautiful, instruments of evil omen, a judgment the last war has proved.
The psalm says that no king is saved by the multitude of an host, and a horse is a vain thing for safety.
James asks where wars and fightings come from, and traces them to the lusts that war within.
Longfellow reckoned that half the wealth bestowed on camps and courts would leave no need of arsenals nor forts.
Clausewitz calls war a mere continuation of policy by other means. Is war only consumption, or an instrument that states choose for their ends?
John sees a pale horse whose rider is Death, with power to kill with sword and with hunger.
David's lament over Saul and Jonathan gives the refrain for every such field: how are the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle.
Jeremiah is pained at his very heart at the trumpet and the alarm of war: destruction upon destruction is cried.
Arnold sees the world as a darkling plain with neither certitude nor peace nor help for pain.
Yeats saw things fall apart and the centre fail to hold, mere anarchy loosed upon the world.
Jeremiah cries to the sword, how long will it be ere thou be quiet? put up thyself into thy scabbard.
Pascal noted that men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as when they do it from religious conviction.
The Preacher lists a time of war and a time of peace among the seasons of life. Is war a pretext that can be removed, or a season that returns?
The Athenians tell the Melians that right is in question only between equals in power. Is war a disease of history, or the way power has always behaved?
William James observed that showing war's irrationality and horror has no effect on its defenders. Why has strife prevailed so long if everyone can see its ruin?
Twain's stranger tells a congregation that in praying for victory they have prayed for all that must follow victory.
Lincoln observed that both sides read the same Bible and pray to the same God, and each invokes his aid against the other.
The psalm asks God to scatter the people that delight in war.
The song of Moses calls the Lord a man of war. How do scriptures that speak in this way stand beside the saying that God does not want war?
Augustine held that war should be waged only as a necessity, and only that peace may be obtained. Is war never necessary, or sometimes the lesser evil?
The Qur’an permits fighting those who fight you and forbids beginning hostilities. Are both parties always in the wrong?
Pericles says of the fallen that heroes have the whole earth for their tomb. What is owed to the devotion of those who die in wars the readings condemn?
Jesus says that greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Socrates says that if he must choose between them, he would rather suffer injustice than do it.
Tennyson's soldiers were not to make reply nor to reason why, only to do and die.
Wilson called for a general association of nations giving mutual guarantees to great and small states alike.
Jeremiah speaks of those who heal the hurt slightly, saying peace, peace, when there is no peace.
Tacitus records the verdict on an empire's peace: they make a solitude and call it peace.
Hugo told a peace congress that a day will come when the nations of the Continent blend into a higher unity.
The Qur’an gives the same rule for believers: make peace between two parties, and if one wrongs the other, fight the one that does wrong until it returns.
Jesus pictures a king who counts his forces, sends an embassy and asks conditions of peace.
Kant preferred many independent states to their fusion under one power that has overgrown the rest. What keeps a pact enforced by all governments from becoming that power?
Isaiah says that the work of righteousness shall be peace, and its effect quietness and assurance.
Augustine defines the peace of all things as the tranquillity of order.
Isaiah's vision is the charter of the hope: swords beaten into plowshares, and nations learning war no more.
The Haudenosaunee Great Law set a Tree of the Great Peace whose roots any nation may follow to shelter.
Zechariah foresees chariot, horse and battle bow cut off, and a king who speaks peace unto the heathen.
Hosea has God promise to break the bow and the sword out of the earth and make them lie down safely.
Machiavelli observed that all armed prophets have conquered and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. Who keeps the peace once arms are reduced to internal security?
Micah adds to the plowshares a picture of what disarmament buys: every man under his vine and fig tree, unafraid.
Isaiah pronounces woe on those who stay on horses and trust in chariots because they are many.
Jesus blesses the peacemakers, who shall be called the children of God.
The women at Seneca Falls rewrote the Declaration to say that all men and women are created equal.
UNESCO's charter holds that since wars begin in the minds of men, the defences of peace must be built there.
The psalm joins the two tasks: depart from evil and do good, seek peace and pursue it.
Santayana warned that those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
Paul's counsel is modest and exacting: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
The Preacher holds that the thing that hath been is that which shall be. After six thousand years of war, what grounds are there for expecting it to cease?
Hillel asks his students to be disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace.
The psalmist has long dwelt with those who hate peace: I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war.
Isaiah sets against every battle of the warrior the birth of a child who shall be called the Prince of Peace.
Jesus tells the disciple who drew a sword to put it up, for all who take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Joel has the reverse of Isaiah's call, the summons the reading sees obeyed: beat your plowshares into swords.
The Qur’an holds that whoever kills a human being unjustly, it is as if he had killed all mankind.
Jesus beholds a city and says, if thou hadst known the things which belong unto thy peace.
The psalm calls God a refuge and strength, though the earth be removed and the mountains shake.
Kant thought that out of such crooked material as man is made of, nothing can be hammered quite straight.
Proverbs counts the one who rules his spirit better than he that takes a city.
Paul writes to friends he cannot reach that though absent in the flesh he is with them in the spirit.
Paul tells a church from which he was cut off that he was taken from them in presence, not in heart.
Paul thanks God upon every remembrance of friends from whom he is separated.
The psalm praises the one who makes wars to cease unto the end of the earth and breaks the bow.
Lincoln fondly hoped and fervently prayed that the mighty scourge of war might speedily pass away.
Isaiah pictures a hiding place from the wind and a covert from the tempest.
Lincoln asked a nation after war to act with malice toward none, with charity for all, and to bind up its wounds.
The angels' song over Bethlehem joins the two: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace.
Kipling warned an empire that its navies melt away and its pomp is one with Nineveh and Tyre.
Dickinson says that peace is taught by its battles told, as water is taught by thirst.
The emperor Ashoka declared in an edict that even those who do wrong should be forgiven where forgiveness is possible.
The psalm pictures mercy and truth met together, righteousness and peace kissing each other.
Mozi taught that princes who regarded another's kingdom as their own would have no battlefields.
Proverbs says that when a man's ways please the Lord, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.
Isaiah promises perfect peace to the one whose mind is stayed on God.
Jesus leaves his disciples a peace not given as the world gives, and tells them not to be afraid.
Paul says that the weapons of his warfare are not carnal, though mighty for pulling down strongholds.
Paul promises a peace of God which passes all understanding to keep hearts and minds.
Blake vows not to cease from mental fight, a war of another kind for another city.
Paul arms the believer with the whole armour of God, to withstand and having done all to stand.
Shakespeare's king says that in peace nothing so becomes a man as modest stillness, and in war the action of the tiger. What should a colonel leave behind with the battle line, and what keep?
Jesus asks that a light so shine before men that they see good works and glorify God.
Zechariah is told that it is not by might, nor by power, but by the spirit of the Lord.
Elisha's servant has his eyes opened and sees the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire, an army no enemy counted.
Isaiah foresees the wolf dwelling with the lamb, and a little child leading them.
Swift remarked that we have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.
The priestly blessing ends as this prayer does: the Lord lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.

isaiah-prince-of-peace.text: For every battle of the warrior is with confused noise, and garments rolled in blood; but this shall be with burning and fuel of fire. For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace

psalm-scatter-the-people-that-delight-in.text: scatter thou the people that delight in war

psalm-teacheth-my-hands-to-war.text: Blessed be the Lord my strength which teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight

hosea-break-the-bow-and-the-sword.text: And in that day will I make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field and with the fowls of heaven, and with the creeping things of the ground: and I will break the bow and the sword and the battle out of the earth, and will make them to lie down safely

zechariah-battle-bow-shall-be-cut-off.text: And I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off: and he shall speak peace unto the heathen: and his dominion shall be from sea even to sea, and from the river even to the ends of the earth

luke-conditions-of-peace.text: Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace

samuel-shall-the-sword-devour-for-ever.text: Then Abner called to Joab, and said, Shall the sword devour for ever? knowest thou not that it will be bitterness in the latter end? how long shall it be then, ere thou bid the people return from following their brethren

jeremiah-sword-of-the-lord-how-long.text: O thou sword of the Lord, how long will it be ere thou be quiet? put up thyself into thy scabbard, rest, and be still

psalm-no-king-saved-by-the-multitude-of-.text: There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength. An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength

isaiah-woe-to-them-that-trust-in-chariot.text: Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the Lord

ecclesiastes-a-time-of-war.text: A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace

proverbs-enemies-to-be-at-peace.text: When a man's ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him
